args.diagnosis: Domain classification: app — image-provider slowness is application-level (serving large images), not caused by synchronous upstream calls/timeouts.
args.reasoning: 1) pod list: image-provider-79dbdd7cf4-gnmjv is Running (functions.get_pods_from_service). 2) Pod logs show many successful GETs with large response sizes (e.g., 347245, 369585 bytes) and HTTP 200s but no repeated timeout or error messages (~500 lines inspected) — indicates the container is serving images locally, not failing on remote calls (functions.get_logs). 3) Deployment/pod spec contains no environment variables or command args pointing to an external image store/generator or a client timeout setting (only OTEL and IMAGE_PROVIDER_PORT are present) (functions.kubectl_get & functions.kubectl_describe). 4) Tracing query returned no error traces for image-provider in the lookback window (functions.get_traces). Together these unique findings rule out the hypothesis that image-provider is blocking on an upstream remote image store with ~10s timeouts; the evidence points to application-level behavior (large payload delivery or client/network transfer time) causing ~10s spans.

final_report.root_cause: Misconfigured Envoy (frontend-proxy) upstream handling: the frontend-proxy’s Envoy configuration lacks appropriate upstream/request timeouts, connection/request limits and defensive retry/outlier handling for the image-provider cluster. Envoy therefore blocks and queues client requests while waiting on variable/slower responses from image-provider, producing large tail latencies (~10s) and non-trivial internal processing tails (~2.8–3s). This proxy behavior was amplified by image-provider running as a single replica with tight memory (50Mi) and serving large image payloads, producing variable response times that triggered the proxy queuing/blocking behavior.
final_report.evidence_summary: 1) Traces: many frontend-proxy root spans show long tails (2.8–3s) and multiple traces with ~10s total latency where frontend-proxy calls image-provider (response_flags DI,DC; http.status_code=0 in Envoy span) indicating upstream connection/response problems. 2) Envoy logs: warnings about missing downstream connection limits and normal cluster initialization ('loading 13 cluster(s)') — config gaps present. 3) Pod/service inspection: frontend-proxy is a single running pod (frontend-proxy-55b6b6c7d9-mwgnk) with no CPU/memory saturation, and image-provider is a single pod (image-provider-79dbdd7cf4-gnmjv) serving large image payloads (logs show successful 200s with payloads ~300–370KB) and a 50Mi memory limit. 4) Connectivity checks: image-provider Service and Endpoints match the frontend-proxy configuration (IMAGE_PROVIDER_HOST=image-provider, port 8081) — DNS/port mismatch ruled out. Together these show Envoy’s upstream handling, not DNS/port misconfiguration or image-provider application errors, is the primary failure point, with image-provider resource/config contributing to variability.
final_report.investigation_summary: Priority-weighted investigation focused first on frontend-proxy/Envoy (priority #1) and traced long tail latencies to Envoy spans targeting image-provider; Envoy span flags (DI,DC) and admin/log warnings pointed to upstream connection/handling issues rather than pod resource exhaustion. Priority #2 validated that DNS/port mapping between frontend-proxy and image-provider is correct, eliminating misconfigured host/port as the cause. Priority #3 inspected image-provider and found it serves large images successfully but runs as a single replica with a low memory limit, which can cause variable response durations. Correlating traces, logs, metrics and pod configs produced a causal chain implicating Envoy configuration as the root cause, amplified by the image-provider deployment footprint and payload sizes. No further probing tasks were required to reach a confident root cause.
